title: Advanced Infrastructure
description: Explore Kubernetes scheduling, chaos engineering, blue-green and canary deployments, and feature flags for safe, scalable infrastructure.

segments.text: Building software is one thing. Running it reliably at scale is another challenge entirely. Today we cover the advanced infrastructure patterns that keep production systems alive.

Kubernetes orchestrates containers across a cluster. The scheduler decides which node runs each pod based on resource requests, node affinity, taints, and tolerations. It is a constraint satisfaction problem.
The scheduler filters nodes that cannot run the pod, then scores the remaining ones. Scoring considers resource balance, data locality, and pod spreading. The highest-scoring node wins.

Blue-green deployment runs two identical environments. Blue serves production traffic. Green gets the new version. Once green passes health checks, the load balancer switches traffic instantly. Rollback is just switching back.

Canary deployment is more cautious. Route one percent of traffic to the new version first. Monitor error rates and latency. Gradually increase to ten, then fifty, then a hundred percent. Any spike means automatic rollback.

segments.thought_prompt: Blue-green requires double the infrastructure. Canary is slower to roll out. When would you choose each?

segments.text: Feature flags decouple deployment from release. Ship code to production but hide it behind a flag. Enable it for internal users first, then beta testers, then everyone. No redeployment needed to toggle features.

Chaos engineering proactively injects failures into production. Kill a random pod. Introduce network latency. Simulate a zone outage. If your system survives, you have confidence. If not, you found a weakness before your users did.

Netflix pioneered this with Chaos Monkey. The process: define steady state, hypothesize what happens during failure, inject the failure, observe. If the hypothesis is wrong, you have a real resilience gap to fix.

None of this works without observability. Metrics tell you what is happening. Logs tell you why. Traces tell you where in the distributed call chain. Together, they form the three pillars you need to operate safely.
Here is a scenario to consider.
segments.thought_prompt: Your canary deployment shows a 0.5% increase in error rate. Is that noise or a real problem? How would you decide?

segments.text: You need statistical significance. Compare error rates with a chi-squared test or use a pre-set threshold with a minimum sample size. Advanced infrastructure is not just about tools. It is about building systems and processes that make failure safe and deployments boring. That is the goal.
